h1: Prefab Labour Camps: Repeatable Blocks for Site Camps
seoTitle: Prefab Labour Camps: Six Repeatable Block Sizes | SAMAN
metaDescription: Prefab labour camps supplied as repeatable blocks. Six sizes from 200 to 900 sq ft, each priced separately. Panel build, plug-in services, phased expansion.
opener: Prefab labour camps from SAMAN are supplied as repeatable accommodation blocks rather than as one finished settlement. You buy a block, and you repeat it around a service spine as the workforce grows. Each block leaves our Bengaluru or Greater Noida works as a bolted steel bay frame clad in insulated sandwich panel, with services routed to a single connection point so a plot can be added or taken out of use without disturbing the rest of the camp. Six block sizes are published, from 200 to 900 sq ft, and each carries its own rate. Anything above 900 sq ft of covered area is quoted manually by block mix, because at that point the external infrastructure drives the cost rather than the buildings do.
descriptionHtml:
What a repeatable camp block actually is

A prefab labour camp block is a complete, self-contained building that leaves the factory finished and arrives on site ready to connect. It is not a kit of panels assembled in place, and it is not a converted shipping container. The structure is a bolted light steel bay frame on pedestals or a strip plinth, clad in insulated sandwich panel. The roof is insulated panel or PPGI sheet with a proper ridge, eave and gutter line.

The word that matters in the product name is repeatable. Every block we make for a camp shares one bay spacing, one panel module, one door and window family and one service interface. That sounds like a manufacturing convenience, and it is. But the benefit lands on your site rather than in our works, because we reproduce blocks batch after batch without redrawing anything. A damaged panel on the fourth block is the same panel as on the first. A door that fails in year three comes from stock rather than from a fabricator matching it.

It also means the camp is not a single object. It is a set of components on a grid, and the grid is the product.

How the six sizes change the camp plan

The six published sizes fall into two families, and the split between them is more useful to a planner than the areas are.

The 10 ft wide family: 20x10, 30x10 and 40x10 ft

Everything at 10 ft wide behaves the same way in transport, in lifting and in setting out. These three sizes travel on standard trailers, need the same working margin around the plot, and use the same spares. They are single-volume or simply partitioned buildings, and cross ventilation through opposite walls works because the room is never deep. Most camps buy several of these before they buy anything wider.

The 20 ft wide family: 30x20, 40x20 and 45x20 ft

At 20 ft the building changes character. The floor needs an internal support line. The plot needs a wider footprint with margin on both sides. Inside, rooms can sit off a circulation route instead of forming one volume. These sizes are where sanitation blocks, canteens and mixed-use blocks live. They also carry the lower rates, because the frame and the services spread across more floor area.

Rates fall as the block grows. A 200 sq ft block runs at Rs 1,150 per sq ft; a 900 sq ft block runs at Rs 900. That is not a volume discount on the same product. It reflects the fact that a longer, wider block reuses one connection point, one roof drainage run and one base frame across more usable floor.

What the quoted rate covers, and what it does not

This is the part most quotations leave vague, so we state it plainly.

Included in the published rate

  • The block enclosure: frame, floor, walls, roof, insulation, doors and windows
  • Standard services-ready fit-out: internal wiring in conduit, protection, lighting and fan points, and a single service interface for water, waste and power
  • Factory quality checks, dimensional inspection, coating touch-up and dispatch protection

Not included, quoted separately when you need it

  • Loose beds, bunks, lockers and any furniture
  • Kitchen equipment and canteen fit-out
  • External sanitation plant, septic systems and sewer connection
  • Foundations, plinths, pedestals and site levelling
  • Transport, offloading, positioning and erection
  • Utility distribution across the camp, and the service spine itself
  • Statutory approvals and project-specific structural or performance engineering

A block that arrives with beds in it has been quoted with beds in it. Nothing here assumes otherwise. Where an interior image shows bunk frames, it shows a fitted example rather than the standard supply.

The service spine, and why blocks are planned around it

Camps that fail operationally usually fail on services, not on buildings. Water reaches the dormitories but not the wash block. Waste from the canteen crosses the pedestrian route. A repair to one drain shuts down half the camp because nothing can be isolated.

We plan camps around a service spine for that reason. Water, waste and power run along one route, and every block connects to it at a single interface with its own isolation. The consequences are practical. A block can be taken out of service without touching its neighbours. A new plot can be trenched and connected before its building arrives. Zones can be metered and watched separately, so a leak shows up as a reading rather than as a flood.

Zoning follows the same logic. Dormitory, sanitation, canteen and supervisor or admin functions sit in defined zones, and pedestrian movement is kept clear of service vehicle routes. On a camp that runs three shifts, that separation is a safety measure rather than a layout preference.

Panels, roof and floor: one assembly chosen per block type

The specification allows nominal 50, 60 or 80 mm PUF, EPS or mineral-wool panels. We select one panel family per block type on the project brief, and we do not mix them within a block. Climate drives part of that choice and the project fire strategy drives the rest. Thicker is not automatically better. Core, facing, joint detail and ventilation all matter more than the number on the datasheet.

Roofs are insulated panel or PPGI with a defined ridge, eave, flashing and gutter run. In hot climates we plan the ventilation or ceiling strategy alongside the insulation, not after it. A thick roof panel on its own does not fix a hot dormitory. Ceiling fans, ridge and eave airflow and condensation risk are considered together.

Floors are where the two block types genuinely diverge. Dry blocks such as dormitories and admin rooms use a bolted steel joist deck with a cement board or ply platform, finished in commercial vinyl. Wet blocks such as toilets, wash areas and kitchens use a waterproof cementitious or RCC substrate with an epoxy, tile or safety finish. That is a deliberate split, not an inconsistency, and it has a consequence worth knowing before you plan a move.

Moving the camp, and what actually moves

Dry blocks are designed to be demounted and relocated. Wet blocks depend on fixed site civil work, drainage falls and connections that cannot travel with the building. Any supplier who tells you an entire camp lifts and moves as one is describing a sales pitch rather than a wet block.

A planned demobilisation runs as a sequence. Services are isolated block by block at the spine. Interiors are cleared and the packing list is checked against the original bill of materials. Blocks are disconnected, inspected for reuse, and lifted or loaded on the approved lifting and support points shown on the general arrangement drawing. Panels, trims and fixings that will be reused are recorded; those that will not are noted so the next site is quoted honestly.

We do not publish a number of moves. It depends on handling discipline, lifting method, exposure at each site, and how well the crew maintained seals and coatings in between. What we will do is inspect a returning block and tell you what it needs before it goes out again.

What your site has to be ready for

The block is our scope. The ground it stands on is yours, and camps are delayed by ground far more often than by buildings.

  • Level, compacted ground with working margin on all sides of each plot
  • Foundations, plinths or pedestals set out and cured to the approved drawing
  • Access for a trailer and for the offloading method agreed in the quotation
  • The service spine trenched, and water, waste and power available at the block interface
  • Drainage falls established, particularly around wet blocks
  • Statutory approvals in place for the camp as a whole

Sort the plot and the spine before delivery. That one step does more than anything else to keep an installation to days rather than weeks.

Where the block ladder stops and a project quotation begins

Every size on this page is priced by area rate. Above 900 sq ft of covered area we stop doing that, and we say so rather than extrapolating.

The reason is that beyond a certain size the cost of a camp is no longer mostly the buildings. Water storage and pumping, sewage treatment or septic capacity, power distribution and standby, roads and drainage, boundary and security, and the approvals all start to dominate. Multiplying a per-square-foot rate by a larger number produces a figure that looks precise and is wrong. So a larger camp is quoted manually, by block mix and by external infrastructure scope.

Two alternatives are worth knowing about. Our labour sheds page covers one large open dormitory hall. That is a cheaper way to house a big crew when the building stays put and privacy is not a requirement. For small partitioned rooms below 200 sq ft, labour hutments fits better.

A note on two-storey blocks

Stacking a block to G+1 is a separate engineered package. It brings its own frame, staircase and access walkway design, and it is not included in the single-storey rates published on this page. Tell us at enquiry stage if your plot is tight enough that stacking is the only option. We then quote the engineering with the blocks rather than after them.

What you get at handover

Each block is checked before dispatch and again at handover. Dimensional and member checks come first, then weld and bolt inspection, coating condition, panel fit, roof drainage and every opening. Electrical and plumbing checks follow.

The handover pack names the approved general arrangement drawing and bill of materials, the material schedule, test records where the contract calls for them, photographs, outstanding punch items, the lifting and service-connection data, and the maintenance points. Fire, thermal, acoustic, structural and hygiene performance appear only where the contracted evidence supports them, which on a standard camp block usually means they do not appear at all.

What to send us for a quotation

  • Site location, and access constraints for a trailer
  • Block mix and quantity, by size
  • What each block is for: sleeping, sanitation, canteen, admin or store
  • Project duration, and whether the camp will be relocated
  • Whether foundations, transport, erection and utility distribution are in your scope or ours
  • Any fire, thermal or acoustic requirement your client has specified in writing
  • Required delivery date

We return a fixed-price quotation within 48 hours. Standard delivery is 7 to 21 working days from order confirmation, depending on the block mix and the works loading at the time.

Questions buyers ask about prefab labour camps

What does a prefab labour camp cost in India?

Our published block rates run from Rs 1,150 per sq ft at 200 sq ft down to Rs 900 at 900 sq ft, ex-GST. That covers the block enclosure and services-ready fit-out. Market figures quoted elsewhere vary enormously because they bundle different scopes. Always ask what a rate includes before comparing it.

What is the difference between a labour camp and a labour colony?

In common use they describe the same thing at different scales. On this site, camp means a set of repeatable blocks bought and connected in phases. Colony means a complete settlement planned and priced as one project.

Can blocks be added later?

Yes, and that is the point of the grid. We trench and connect a new plot to the existing spine. The new block then uses the same bay module, panel and service interface as the ones already standing.

Can the camp be moved to the next site?

Dry blocks are designed for demounting and relocation. Wet blocks depend on fixed civil work that stays behind. Plan a move as a block-by-block sequence with a reuse inspection, not as a single lift of the whole camp.

Do we need permission for a prefab camp?

Statutory approvals for worker accommodation are the project's responsibility and vary by state and by client. We supply the drawings and specifications your approval submission needs. We do not certify compliance.

How long does installation take?

Delivery is 7 to 21 working days from order confirmation. Time on site depends on the block mix, the readiness of the plot and the spine, and the offloading method. Ground that is not ready is the usual cause of overrun.
